Modern.brandNameRationale: Case is the box jewelry lives in when you're not wearing it. We named the brand after the moment of safekeeping, not the moment of wearing. One word. Direct. Has weight.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern fine jewelry brands have moved past Tiffany and into a smaller, more design-led market. The customer wants something they could wear daily, that doesn't broadcast price. The category is asking for restraint with personality.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Mejuri (mejuri.com) defined the modern fine jewelry direct-to-consumer playbook. Catbird (catbirdnyc.com) holds the indie craft position. Ana Khouri (anakhouri.com) sits at the top of the design-led contemporary space. We sit closest to Catbird in tone with a sharper visual signature.
Modern.positioningStatement: Modern fine jewelry for people who buy one piece a year and wear it every day.

Modern.tagline: Jewelry that is the past tense.
Modern.brandNameRationale: One word, past tense — a small linguistic move that says 'lived in, kept, on the body'. Worn signals that the piece is meant to be used, not displayed. Reads as quiet and slightly considered.
Modern.manifesto: Most fine jewelry brands sell objects for the safe. We made Worn because the right piece is on the body every day for the next forty years. The brand is the wear, not the unboxing. Pieces are designed to thicken, dull, scratch — to look like something that has been somewhere.
Modern.industrySummary: DTC fine jewelry has consolidated around a polished, pristine, photogenic aesthetic. There is a real opening for a brand that designs for wear rather than against it — patina, scratch, body warmth.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Mejuri (mejuri.com) defined the modern DTC jewelry brand. Catbird (catbirdnyc.com) holds the considered indie slot. Aurate (auratenewyork.com) sits in the polished middle. We sit further out — the wear is the design.
Modern.positioningStatement: Worn is a fine jewelry brand designed for forty years of daily wear, not for the photograph.
Modern.positioningRationale: We design with the patina in mind. The brand documents pieces years into wear, not just on day one. The customer is buying the piece five years from now.

Want to keep the piece a long time.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two surnames, joined by an ampersand. The structure of an English family jeweler from the 1880s. Wentworth and Wynn sound like they could have founded the firm together. The pair carries the heritage the brand wants to claim, without claiming it directly.
Luxury.story: Wentworth & Wynn began in a small workshop above a London street. The two founders, who had spent decades in larger houses, wanted to make a smaller number of pieces, more carefully. The firm has stayed at the same address. The workshop has stayed at the same size.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end jewelry is divided between the grand maisons (Cartier, Van Cleef, Boucheron) and the new design-led contemporary brands. There's a small, durable category between them. Family-run, multi-generational, English-craft jewelers who serve a few hundred clients. We belong there.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Cartier (cartier.com) is the institution. Theo Fennell (theofennell.com) is the closest contemporary English peer. Stephen Webster (stephenwebster.com) has the personality. Bentley & Skinner (bentley-skinner.co.uk) holds the heritage corner. We are quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: An English jeweler that makes a small number of pieces, very carefully.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy, often inherited. Already owns important pieces. Buys for milestones (births, anniversaries, retirements) and expects the piece to be passed on. Values the relationship with the jeweler as much as the piece.

dos: Address the client by surname
Speak in the language of craft, not marketing
Send a paper invitation to every private viewing

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark. Wentworth & Wynn set with elegant ligatures and a hand-drawn ampersand that becomes the firm's hallmark. The W-and-W monogram stamps the inside of every piece, the back of the case, and the wax seal on every paper letter.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Single proper name with the 'House of' prefix — the heritage-jewelry naming convention. Marlbrough is a slightly older English variant spelling that reads as established and slightly archaic. The 'House of' signals workshop, not factory.
Luxury.story: The House of Marlbrough is a single workshop founded in 1934, now run by the founder's granddaughter. The workshop produces fewer than four hundred pieces a year. Each piece is signed and dated by the maker. Most pieces sold today are commissioned, not in catalog.
Luxury.industrySummary: Heritage fine jewelry brands have largely been absorbed into LVMH and Richemont. There is a quieter market for the single-workshop house — small annual production, signed pieces, multi-generational ownership.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Hemmerle (hemmerle.com) is the closest peer in workshop scale and seriousness. JAR (no public site) holds the legendary atelier slot. Cartier (cartier.com) and Van Cleef (vancleefarpels.com) are the conglomerate references. We sit with the single-workshop houses.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A single-workshop fine jewelry house producing fewer than four hundred signed pieces per year, now in its third generation.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not scale. The workshop is the limit. Pieces are signed, dated, and recorded. The customer is buying a piece from a specific maker in a specific year.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Past participle. The thing that jewelry is meant to become. We named the brand after its purpose, not its product. One word. Implies use, not display.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most jewelry brands sell occasion. We sell daily use. The customer wants a piece that comes off only at the shower and goes back on before they leave the house. The category needs a brand that says so plainly.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Many small jewelers operate in this aesthetic space. None have claimed the language as clearly. The Ordinary did it for skincare. We do it for fine jewelry.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Fine jewelry made to be worn every day. Not saved.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: One word. The word every jewelry buyer uses for what they own: 'this piece, that piece'. We named the brand after the unit and stopped. Plain, slightly anonymous, completely honest.
Minimal.manifesto: Jewelry brand vocabulary has run away from the object. Collection, line, edit, drop. We made Piece because the customer already calls it a piece. The product page shows the piece. The price is the price. The packaging says PIECE.

Corporate.tagline: Distribution and licensing for fine jewelry brands.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Halcyon means calm, prosperous, established. The word carries seriousness without trying. Jewelry Group names the category clearly. The whole thing reads like a holding company, which is exactly what it is.
Corporate.industrySummary: Behind every visible jewelry brand sits a quiet network of distributors, licensors, and category managers. The B2B side of fine jewelry is a real category with serious players. The customers are not consumers, they are buyers at jewelry chains, department stores, and licensing partners.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Richemont (richemont.com) holds the maison portfolio. Movado Group (movadogroup.com) sits in the watch and jewelry corporate side. LVMH Watches and Jewelry (lvmh.com) is the giant peer. We are smaller and faster, focused on the contemporary fine jewelry tier rather than the heritage maisons.
Corporate.positioningStatement: A jewelry holding company building the next generation of fine jewelry brands.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Independent jewelry brands need scale partners. Department stores need a single vendor across multiple labels. We sit in the middle, professionalizing what was previously a fragmented B2B space.

Corporate.tagline: Wholesale and trade fine jewelry, established 1968.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Renwick is a Scottish surname with a goldsmithing register. Goldsmith Ltd. is the trade name and corporate form. The pair reads as an established jewelry trade firm — the kind that supplies retailers and corporate clients, not consumers.
Corporate.manifesto: Renwick Goldsmith Ltd. is a wholesale and trade jewelry firm supplying retail jewelers, corporate gifting programs, and bespoke trade orders since 1968. The buyer is a retail buyer, a corporate gifting director, or a jewelry house seeking white-label production. The relationship is the multi-year contract.
Corporate.industrySummary: Trade jewelry supply has consolidated under a small number of integrated suppliers. The opening is for a long-standing trade firm with deep workshop capacity, transparent pricing, and the operational reliability buyers and corporate gifting teams demand.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Stuller (stuller.com) is the U.S. trade supply reference. Cooksongold (cooksongold.com) is the European peer. Quality Gold (qgold.com) sits in the broad trade middle. We sit in the heritage trade supplier category with workshop production.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Renwick Goldsmith Ltd. is a trade fine jewelry supplier with in-house workshop capacity, serving retail jewelers and corporate gifting programs since 1968.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on workshop depth, trade pricing transparency, and the consistent operational performance long-standing trade buyers rely on.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Trophy is what you earn and put on display. We named the brand after the act of marking a moment. The word is loud, slightly cheeky, and instantly understood. One word, all caps, looks great stamped on a velvet box.
Creative.manifesto: Most jewelry brands ask you to think of jewelry as art or as investment or as inheritance. We think jewelry is closer to a trophy. Something you earn, something you wear, something you point at when someone asks. The piece is a mark on your timeline.
Creative.industrySummary: Fine jewelry has been earnest and quiet. The customer who wants the piece to be loud, playful, and personal hasn't been served by a single brand cleanly. There's room for one that turns the wedding-band-and-watch occasion into a wider trophy economy.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Catbird (catbirdnyc.com) does indie playful. Foundrae (foundrae.com) does meaning-charged pieces. Brent Neale (brentneale.com) has the candy maximalism. We are punchier than any of them and more direct about what the jewelry is for.
Creative.positioningStatement: Jewelry for moments you actually want to remember.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Buys jewelry for themselves to mark moments (job change, divorce, deal close, milestone birthday). Wears the piece. Tells the story when asked. Doesn't wait for someone else to gift it.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words said in the voice of someone passing down something good. Keep This is an instruction, a small command, a hand-off. It names what the customer should do with the piece for the rest of their life. Warm, slightly cinematic, slightly insistent.
Creative.manifesto: Most fine jewelry brands sell aspiration. We made Keep This because the actual value of a piece of jewelry is in being kept — passed down, worn into the metal, brought back to a granddaughter forty years from now. The whole brand is built around that arc. We engrave the instruction on the box.
Creative.industrySummary: DTC jewelry markets on novelty and aspirational lifestyle. There is room for a brand that markets on permanence — the piece kept across generations, the box engraved with the recipient's name.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Catbird (catbirdnyc.com) plays in the considered indie space. Anna Sheffield (annasheffield.com) holds the heirloom-minded slot. Otiumberg (otiumberg.com) sits in the modern-minimal peer position. We sit further out — every piece of the brand surface argues for keeping.
Creative.positioningStatement: Keep This is a fine jewelry brand built around the act of keeping — engraved boxes, named recipients, generational records.
Creative.positioningRationale: Every piece ships engraved with a name. The brand maintains a generational register of where pieces end up. The brand is the keeping, not the buying.

behaviors: Buy jewelry for milestones — birth, marriage, anniversary.

Care about the box and the engraving.
Tell the story of the piece every time they wear it.
motivations: Want a piece that will be kept.

messagingPillars.description: We maintain a record of every piece and its current keeper. If the piece is passed down, the register is updated. The brand follows the piece.

messagingPillars.name: Repair forever
messagingPillars.description: We repair every piece we have ever sold, for as long as the workshop exists. Repair is a flat fee, published.

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — KEEP THIS engraved in a quiet display serif, paired with a small etched line beneath, like a signature. Used directly on the wooden box at small scale.

colorPalette.name: Gold
colorPalette.meaning: Single accent — the engraved year mark.
colorPalette.usage: The year mark on the box and certificate.

typography.primary: A quiet display serif for the wordmark and engraving.
typography.secondary: A book serif for the certificate and printed register.
typography.rationale: Engraver's register. The brand is meant to be read as something old, even on day one.

Creative.brandDescription: Keep This is a fine jewelry brand built around the act of keeping — engraved boxes, named recipients, generational records.
Creative.mission: Every piece ships engraved with a name. The brand maintains a generational register of where pieces end up. The brand is the keeping, not the buying.
Creative.vision: We engrave the instruction on the box.
coreValues: Warm — we are friendly, not formal.
Specific — generalities are how people avoid commitment.
Considered — we choose fewer things, more carefully.
Slightly cinematic — a core principle the brand operates by.
Creative.scope:
KEEP THIS works across:
• Engraved boxes
• Generational register
• Repair forever
